title: Weather App
description: Design a weather app — ingesting data from providers, serving current conditions and forecasts by location with aggressive caching, and pushing severe-weather alerts.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Weather App?
blocks.text: A weather app shows current conditions and forecasts for a user's location or saved cities, and alerts users about severe weather nearby.

items: Users should see current weather and a 7-day forecast for their location or a searched city.
Users should be able to save favourite locations.
Users should receive push alerts for severe weather in their saved locations.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Fast responses (< 200ms) and very high availability — people check weather constantly.
Data freshness: current conditions within ~10-15 minutes; forecasts hourly.
Scale to 50M daily users with spikes during storms.
Severe-weather alerts delivered within a minute or two.
**Location cell**: a grid cell (e.g. geohash precision 5, ~5km) that weather is computed for.
**Observation / forecast**: weather data for a cell and time.
**Alert**: a severe-weather warning covering a geographic polygon.

blocks.text: 1) Users see current weather and forecasts

An **Ingestion Service** pulls data from weather providers (national weather services, commercial APIs) on a schedule, normalises it, and writes it keyed by **location cell**. The **Weather API** snaps the user's coordinates to a cell and returns that cell's data.
Saved locations live in a user table keyed by user ID, with the cell ID stored alongside for alert matching.

Providers publish alerts with polygons. An **Alert Service** finds which cells intersect the polygon, looks up users whose saved locations (or last known locations) fall in those cells, and sends push notifications through the notification system.
1) How do we serve millions of requests cheaply?

approach.text: Proxy each user request to a weather provider.

challenges.text: Expensive (providers charge per call), slow, and fails when the provider throttles us.

approach.text: Cache provider responses keyed by lat/lng.

challenges.text: Every user has slightly different coordinates, so the hit rate is terrible.

blocks.title: Snap to cells and cache at the edge

approach.text: Round coordinates to a geohash cell so everyone in a neighbourhood shares one cache entry. Pre-fetch data for all populated cells on a schedule rather than on demand, and serve `GET /weather?cell=...` through a CDN with a TTL matching the data freshness (e.g. 10 minutes). Storm spikes are then absorbed by the edge.

challenges.text: Cell size trades precision for hit rate — ~5km is plenty for weather.

blocks.text: 2) How do we deliver alerts quickly to the right people?

Index saved locations by cell ID so "who is in these cells?" is a fast lookup. Expand alert polygons to cells once, fan out notifications through a queue, and deduplicate so users don't receive the same alert for multiple saved places. Prioritise severe alerts ahead of marketing notifications.

quiz.question: Why snap coordinates to geohash cells?
options: So nearby users share one cache entry, raising hit rates
quiz.explanation: Exact coordinates are nearly unique per user.

quiz.question: Why not call the weather provider on every request?
options: It's slow, costly per call, and subject to provider throttling
quiz.explanation: Pre-fetching and caching decouple traffic from provider calls.

quiz.question: How do you find users affected by a severe-weather alert?
options: Convert the alert polygon to cells and look up saved locations by cell
quiz.explanation: A cell index makes the lookup fast.

quiz.question: What should the CDN TTL match?
quiz.explanation: Caching longer than the refresh interval would serve stale data.
